Gamers around the world got their first taste of "Grand Theft Auto VI" this week, as critics heaped praise on one of the most anticipated video game releases ever.

The latest instalment of the crime franchise comes 13 years after the last full edition broke sales records and became one of the most profitable entertainment products of all time.

The series lets players live out gangster fantasies, smash up cars and fight whoever they choose in a fictionalised US city populated by lowlifes, sex workers and thugs.

"GTA VI" launched first in New Zealand at midnight local time (1200 CET on Wednesday) and is rolling out around the world as each market reaches midnight.

New Zealander Luke Starik was among the first to play, and his character did not last long. "Wasted already. First one, didn't survive long," he told the AFP news agency, laughing.

"This is one of the big things in my life...I've been playing GTA for such a long time," Riley Fennel, an Australian student visiting Tokyo, told AFP.

Review aggregator Metacritic gave the game a score of 99 out of 100.

A 42-year-old gamer wrote on a German-language Reddit forum that he had taken time off work to play all night. By 1:20 am, he was already in bed with a headache, still blown away by the game.

"Thirteen years ago, with a game like this, I'd have played until six in the morning," the gamer wrote.

In the game's official Reddit forum, people raved about improved interactive elements, such as being able to push a stranded ski jet back in the water.

"This is amazing!" one person wrote.

Analytics firm Omdia estimates "GTA VI" could generate $3.2 billion (€2.9 billion) in sales by the end of the year for studio Rockstar Games and parent company Take-Two Interactive.

PlayStation briefly reported connection issues on its status page before services were restored.

'Taylor Swift of games'

In a review for The Verge titled "GTA VI does something impossible - it lives up to the hype," Andrew Webster wrote that "the game is so good that the outsize hype is the least interesting thing about it."

Social media users praised the graphics.

"There's one moment, no spoilers, where the light hits behind one of the characters just right, and I swore I was looking at a real human," wrote Reddit user No_Strike9652.

Before the release, Joost van Dreunen, a professor at New York University's Stern School of Business, told AFP the game was an "outlier" in the entertainment industry.

"This is the Taylor Swift of video games," he said.

"The reach of the game is such that it will lead to a downstream effect on engagement on other entertainment services," such as streaming platforms, said Omdia analyst James McWhirter.

Many fans have taken time off to explore the fictional state of Leonida, which is modelled on Florida.

"I'm going to take four days off," said Dmytro Shkambara, a 27-year-old Ukrainian player living in Berlin, who said he had been planning his first session "for a very long time."

Human resources platform Remote said it had seen a 32% increase in leave requests worldwide for 19 November.

Billed as bigger, better and more realistic than its predecessors, "GTA VI" follows a Bonnie-and-Clyde-style couple trying to survive in Vice City, a crime-ridden city modelled on Miami.

The game received eight nominations on Tuesday for the Game Awards, the US ceremony honouring the year's best video games, which takes place on 10 December.

Subversion and controversy

Rockstar spent more than eight years developing the game.

The studio delayed the launch twice after a 2022 hack in which stolen gameplay footage was posted online, and it was hit by another round of leaks last summer.

The series has long been accused of glorifying violence and crime. It has also become a pop culture symbol of subversion, known for mocking the flaws of American society.

Players can run over pedestrians, sell drugs and shoot at police.

"It's a series that is famous for being always over the top in terms of its representation of violence and different forms of abuse or harassment, for its representations of gender," said Paolo Ruffino, a lecturer in digital cultures at King's College London.

"I don't expect to see necessarily major controversies unless there is something completely new," he added.

No official release is currently planned in Russia, China, Lebanon or Qatar.

Pierce Brosnan has welcomed Robert Pattinson into the exclusive 007 club by telling the newly-announced seventh Bond to "enjoy the ride".

Brosnan was the fifth actor to portray Bond, starting with GoldenEye in 1995. He went on to star in three more films: Tomorrow Never Dies (1997), The World Is Not Enough (1999), and Die Another Day (2002).

In an Instagram post early today, Brosnan assured Pattinson he would make a “magnificent” Bond.

He wrote: “Dear Robert, Welcome to the world of Bond. You are going to be magnificent. I have fond memories of our time together making ‘Remember Me’. It has been a joy to watch you create a remarkable body of work and to go from strength to strength."

Brosnan and Pattinson starred alongside each other in the 2010 romantic-drama film Remember Me.

Brosnan concluded: “Enjoy the ride. Grá mor, Pierce.”

View this post on Instagram

Actors including Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, Callum Turner and Nicholas Hoult were reported to be in contention for the role before Pattinson was unveiled as the man who follows in the footsteps of only six actors to have played James Bond on the big screen – Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Brosnan and Craig.

Brosnan had previously given his backing to Turner, and earlier this week, Lazenby - the oldest living 007 actor – also welcomed Pattinson into the fold.

The 87-year-old, who played Bond once in 1969’s On Her Majesty’s Secret Service, posted a video message on Instagram.

Vincent van Gogh's painting "Chestnut Trees in Bloom", has fetched a record €173 million at Sotheby's in New York, the most expensive sale for a work by the Dutch artist. It is the fourth most expensive artwork ever sold at auction.

A masterpiece by Vincent van Gogh has sold for a record-setting €173 million at an auction in New York.

The Dutch artist painted "Chataigniers en fleurs" (Chestnut Trees in Blossom) in 1890 in Auvers-sur-Oise, France.

The work dates from an extraordinary period of creative intensity that marked the final two months of van Gogh's life.

According to Sotheby's the sale was organised to settle a long-running row between the seller and the heirs of a previous Jewish owner who sold it in the Nazi era.

Influential German publisher, Samuel Fischer, acquired the painting in Paris in 1909 and his family sold it in 1936. His heirs had previously opposed the sale, saying Fischer's family parted with the painting only because of financial losses suffered under the Nazis.

The Blaquier family acquired the painting in 1975 and has owned it for more than half a century.

The heirs' Berlin-based lawyer, Gunnar Schnabel, had called on Sotheby's to prove the painting was sold at its market value and that the family would have sold it regardless of the political context.

But on Tuesday, Sotheby's said "an agreement has been reached between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and all of the legal descendants of Hedwig and Samuel Fischer regarding the sale.

The previous auction record for a painting by Van Gogh was €106.5 million for the 1888 "Orchard with Cypresses" at Christie's in New York in November 2022.

The inaugural list from TIME crowned the UAE flag carrier Emirates as the best overall, despite travel disruption in the Middle East over the past nine months.

TIME has just unveiled its inaugural list of the world’s best airlines for 2027 – and Emirates took the top spot.

The ranking was based on passenger surveys, with those polled asked to rate their experience on up to five airlines they had flown with over the past three years. They were quizzed on elements like cabin comfort, service quality, entertainment, value for money and the food and beverage offering.

This data, which was collected by intelligence provider Statista, was then combined with an airline’s operational performance from travel data company OAG for an overall rating.

Despite travel disruption in the Middle East in 2026, Emirates also led in the rankings for best value and business travel airlines.

“Undeterred by the challenges of this year, we continue to invest in product and service across almost every touchpoint,” Emirates Airline president Sir Tim Clark said. “We will maintain that focus because, as this top ranking in TIME shows, customers notice when an airline gets the fundamentals right.”

The best airlines in Europe

No European airline broke into the top 10 for TIME’s inaugural list, although several made it into the top 20.

Turkish Airlines was the highest ranked in Europe, coming in 14th. Finnair was hot on its tail (fins), coming in 15th, followed by LOT Polish Airlines in 16th, and British Airways in 17th.

The final European carrier to make the top 25 was Iberia in 24th.

It’s not all doom and gloom for European carriers though. Ryanair, Europe’s largest airline, was named most reliable, while Virgin Atlantic took the title for best long-haul travel experience.

EasyJet also came eighth among the most reliable carriers, with Turkish Airlines in 11th, Wizz Air in 12th, British Airways in 15th, Vueling in 21st and Iberia again in 24th.

Turkish Airlines came fifth for long-haul travel, with KLM in ninth, Iberia in 10th, British Airways in 14th, Air France in 17th, Lufthansa in 18th and SWISS in 19th.

In the passenger’s choice category, which was purely based on travellers’ assessments and their willingness to recommend it to others, Switzerland’s Edelweiss placed seventh.

Finnair came out in 13th place, with LOT Polish Airlines in 14th, Turkish Airlines in 16th and British Airways in 21st.

From former OpenAI researchers to a British technology journalist, the people behind the Claude chatbot could each see their fortunes soar even further into the billions when the company goes public.

When shares in Anthropic go on sale for the first time this week, it will be a major moment not just for the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, but for the wider AI industry and the US stock market.

The company's stock market debut – or initial public offering (IPO) – could become one of the world's most valuable companies overnight

Anthropic plans to sell shares for between $70 (€63) and $78 (€71) each, potentially giving the company a total value of more than $1 trillion (€911.61 billion).

That would put it in the same league as retail giant Walmart and banking heavyweight JPMorgan Chase. It would also make Anthropic more valuable than Coca-Cola, IBM, Starbucks, Delta Air Lines and General Motors combined.

Just five years ago, seven people left rival OpenAI and put their faith in Anthropic, which went from a tiny tech start-up to a giant of the industry.

If the shares sell for $78 (€71), each of the seven founders’ shareholdings will be worth at least $18.5bn (€16.86 billion) each, making them among the richest people on the planet.

Here’s what you need to know about each of them.

Dario Amodei, CEO

Dario Amodei was working at OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, when he decided he wanted to take a different approach to developing artificial intelligence.

In 2020, he left the firm, taking his sister Daniela – now Anthropic’s president – and five other colleagues with him to set up Anthropic.

Raised in San Francisco, California, Amodei showed an early aptitude for both academics and athletics, impressing school friends with his intelligence and speed on the running track.

He was also fascinated by big questions around technology and philosophy, including whether machines could one day become conscious and how science might extend human life.

Amodei initially studied physics at Princeton and Stanford universities but switched to biology and biomedical sciences following his father's death from hepatitis C.

Before joining OpenAI, Amodei worked at Chinese technology giant Baidu and Google.

The 43-year-old has said his decision to leave OpenAI was driven by growing concerns that some within the company were putting commercial interests ahead of AI safety.

Daniela Amodei, President

Dario and his sister Daniela were close growing up and later shared a flat in San Francisco with a group of friends.

Daniela followed her brother into OpenAI and joined him when he left to set up Anthropic.

Daniela studied English literature at the University of California, Santa Cruz, before working for Democratic representative Matt Cartwright.

The 39-year-old also worked as head of risk operations at financial services company Stripe.

She now acts as Anthropic's president, a role which allows her to oversee its executive team and lead work across research, engineering and product development, as well as governance and commercial operations.

Tom Brown, Chief Compute Officer

Before joining Anthropic, Tom Brown built his reputation in the AI industry at Google as part of its DeepMind project and OpenAI, where he was part of the team responsible for developing GPT-3, one of the early large language models that paved the way for ChatGPT.

The 39-year-old also has a background in start-ups, having helped launch Grouper, a social app designed to bring groups of friends together for drinks.

Today, Brown oversees Anthropic's computing resources, a crucial part of the business given the enormous processing power needed to train and operate its AI systems.

He has also voiced support for Donald Trump's push to expand data centre infrastructure in the US, arguing that it represents "an enormous source of prosperity".

Jared Kaplan, Chief Science Officer

Jared Kaplan oversees Anthropic's scientific research and technical development as its chief science officer. He also holds an academic position as an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore.

Kaplan, 42, has a PhD in physics from Harvard University and is best known for his work on AI scaling laws. These are mathematical principles which help explain how AI systems tend to improve as they are trained using larger models and greater amounts of data.

Anthropic says his research has helped give companies a way to predict how their AI models will perform as they grow.

Chris Olah, Interpretability Research Lead

Chris Olah, 34, takes a different approach to AI research, focusing on understanding what happens inside artificial intelligence systems and how they arrive at their decisions.

While his role is technically ‘interpretability research lead’, Canadian Olah is known to ask ethical and philosophical questions surrounding the technology.

According to The New York Times, he has spent much of the past year bringing together religious leaders from different faiths to discuss the links between morality and AI.

Before joining Anthropic, Olah worked as a research scientist at Google Brain before moving to OpenAI, where he led research into how AI systems function.

He left the University of Toronto before completing his degree but went on to receive a Thiel Fellowship, which supports promising young people pursuing research and other projects outside traditional university education.

Jack Clark, Head of Public Benefit

Unlike the other Anthropic founders, Jack Clark comes from a journalism rather than a technical background. The 37-year-old is also the only one born outside North America, having grown up in Brighton, UK.

Clark studied English literature and creative writing at the University of East Anglia before moving into technology journalism. He wrote for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register and Bloomberg before joining OpenAI, initially working in communications and later becoming its policy director.

At Anthropic, he serves as head of public benefit and leads the Anthropic Institute, which examines the wider implications of artificial intelligence and its impact on society.

Sam McCandlish, Chief Architect

36-year-old Sam McCandlish is arguably the least visible of Anthropic's co-founders, but, like the others, he’s expected to own around 1.6% of the company once it goes public.

As Anthropic's chief architect, McCandlish works on the technical design of its AI systems as well as the policies intended to reduce the risks posed by the technology.

He previously worked on AI safety at OpenAI.

He has a PhD in physics from Stanford University and an undergraduate degree in mathematics and physics from Brandeis University in Massachusetts.

European small businesses have ambition and creativity, but lack time and budgets. As Kuo Zhang of Alibaba.com writes in an op-ed for Euronews, affordable, ready-to-use AI and global supply chain tools give even solo founders the capabilities of global companies, freeing them to focus on growth.

Harrison Nott, the teenage British founder, started with a simple problem he wanted to solve: cooling down after sport. Developing a towel was his answer. But turning that idea into a viable business meant navigating a maze of operational grind: finding suitable materials, vetting manufacturers, and negotiating with suppliers who could deliver at the right price and quantity.

Those hurdles did not disappear once he had a first product to sell. Expanding his business meant returning to square one: more searches, more comparisons, and more back-and-forth negotiations. The admin was necessary, but it competed directly for the time and focus he needed to innovate and grow.

AI must be genuinely affordable for smaller teams

Harrison’s dilemma goes to the heart of Europe’s small business challenge and explains why the conversation around artificial intelligence needs a reset. If AI is going to empower Europe’s small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), it cannot remain locked behind enterprise price tags—it must be genuinely affordable for smaller teams. A cheap tool means little if it requires weeks of technical setup, and a powerful model is useless if small businesses cannot afford to run it.

A platform can bridge this gap by making end-to-end commercial AI truly affordable for SMEs, giving founders ready-to-use tools that handle real business tasks without breaking the bank.

An adoption gap will quickly become a competitiveness gap

Right now, a stark adoption gap threatens to hold European entrepreneurs back. Eurostat figures show that just 17% of EU enterprises with 10 to 49 employees use AI, compared with 55% of large corporations with 250 or more staff, and that excludes micro-businesses of fewer than 10 people entirely.

We see a similar picture in the UK, where research by Alibaba.com and Small Business Britain found that while 68% of small businesses want to learn what agentic AI can do for of them, only 5% currently use it regularly.

In a European economy where SMEs represent the backbone of employment and innovation, if AI's productivity gains remain locked inside large enterprises with dedicated IT departments, an adoption gap will quickly become a competitiveness gap.

Why small businesses need more than a chatbot

When the European Commission surveyed SMEs on the adopting AI and automated systems, business owners pointed to investment costs, lack of internal expertise and operational uncertainty. In a large corporation, configuring software and double-checking AI outputs can be spread across teams. In a small firm, that burden barriers falls on the founder, competing directly with serving customers and developing products.

That is why generic, conversational AI is no cure-all for SMEs. Small businesses do not need another blank prompt box that requires them to become systems designers. They need agentic AI, systems designed to autonomously execute multi-step workflows, built directly around everyday commercial realities.

Crucially, however, an AI agent is only as effective as the commercial infrastructure behind it. Simplicity requires substance. When a European SME sources a product, a factory's unit price is only part of the picture. To be genuinely useful, an AI system must be plugged into a live global supply chain: able to analyse market trends, vet verified manufacturers, factor in shipping assumptions and European customs duties, and flag compliance requirements.

Moving from a basic chatbot to an AI agent embedded in real trade infrastructure is the difference between an AI that merely writes a sourcing email and an AI that delivers a vetted shortlist of suppliers ready for sign-off.

Delegating the grind, keeping the control

Handing over complex workflows does not mean surrendering control – vital for a small business that cannot afford an expensive mistake. The right agentic AI model reduces daily supervision while preserving human authority where it counts.

In procurement, for instance, researching the market and bargaining over unit prices is not the same as authorizing a financial commitment. Business owners should be able to set the guardrails for supplier outreach and negotiation, see transparently what their AI agent has done, and step in exclusively when it is time to approve orders, payments, and contracts.

For Harrison, that combination of accessible AI and global trade infrastructure changed the trajectory of his company. Using our agentic AI platform for small businesses, integrated with a global supply chain, he handed over the routine procurement grind. He gave the agent a practical brief: find cooling-towel suppliers, compare prices and minimum order quantities, approach the ten most competitive candidates, and negotiate based on potential bulk volumes.

Leveling the global playfield

Genuine progress in the field of AI should be measured by how affordable it is for small businesses and how much work it saves founders in their day-to-day operations. Reliable AI for SMEs should be affordable and capable of handling complex tasks – such as sorting through cluttered emails, detecting payment fraud and booking shipping routes.

European small businesses are full of ambition and creativity, but they lack time and large budgets. Affordable, ready-to-use AI, combined with global supply chain tools, does more than just reduce software costs. It gives a solo founder working from home the operational capabilities of a global company and gives Europe’s small businesses the freedom to focus on their growth.

Kuo Zhang is in charge of the global B2B platform Alibaba.com, which includes, amongst other things, the AI platform Accio. Accio is an AI-powered B2B platform and an autonomous team of agents for product sourcing, market research and e-commerce automation.

The Xi-Trump-Putin trilateral has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference, immortalised in a famous black and white photograph between Winston Churchill, Franklin Roosevelt and Joseph Stalin in Crimea.

From under thick woollen coats and clutching cigarettes and cigars, the three leaders helped shape the post-world order, including the division of Europe into competing spheres of influence.

For the Baltic states — Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia — the legacy of that settlement was particularly painful, as their Soviet occupation and annexation went unchallenged by the Western Allies.

Yalta 2.0? Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide told me Tuesday night that he doesn’t believe the trilateral will result in new international spheres of power. The last thing anyone desires is an “agreement between great leaders to divide the world between them.”

“I'm not suggesting that's going to happen, but I mean this is something we don't want to see,” he said.

Fredrik Wesslau, senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Putin will probably try to discuss Ukraine and find a conclusion to the full-scale invasion. “He wants Russia, the US and China to decide everyone else's geopolitical fate,” he said. “But in the end it’s impossible to decide on the fundamentals of European security without Europeans.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy presciently told the press in November, right before the fresh round of diplomatic overtures recommenced, “We don't want to have Yalta 2.0. The adrenaline and excitement are building behind the scenes at the UN climate talks in Türkiye, negotiators say, as envoys from nearly 200 nations clash over every word and comma ahead of hoped-for agreements on Friday (20 November).

Alliances are being built, AI is being wielded as negotiators from around the world navigate a melting pot of languages, and sneakers are the preferred footwear at the vast COP31 conference venue in Antalya, Türkiye.

"There's a crazy rush of adrenaline because we're in a real bubble of excitement. We're constantly surrounded by people and we sleep very little, five hours a night at most," Belgian negotiator Catherine Windey told news agency AFP.

"At the last two COPs, I ended up getting sick due to fatigue and the air conditioning in the negotiating rooms."

The annual talks aim to bring together countries to review, develop and implement major climate change agreements.

On Monday (16 November), co-host Australia unveiled the first draft of a broad political deal setting out sharply divergent positions on climate policy while calling for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels.

The sweeping 18-page proposal underscores the gulf that nearly 200 nations must bridge to reach consensus on Friday.

And the pace only intensifies as things progress – especially for smaller and poorer countries who are often those most impacted by climate change, and who are faced with the daunting task of rising above the clamour.

"It's exhausting, but we are here to ensure Africa's voice is heard," says Hamda Amin, a representative from Djibouti.

'Genuine emotional bonds are formed' at COP

As ever, alliances are key – and artificial intelligence is proving a crucial tool.

English is the language of COP, and negotiators who speak other languages are harnessing online translators.

The German development agency GIZ developed an AI-based tool called 'NegotiateCOP' to sift through voluminous documents, summarise them, and pinpoint potential allies who share their positions.

Personal ties matter enormously. Negotiators often come from their countries' climate ministries and are deeply committed to the cause.

"Genuine emotional bonds are formed," says Laurence Tubiana, one of the architects of the 2015 Paris COP.

'Geopolitics plays a huge role in the negotiations'

That year saw participating nations adopt the Paris Agreement to keep global warming "well below" 2°C above pre-industrial levels, while pursuing efforts to limit it to 1.5°C to avert the worst impacts of global warming.

Expectations for this COP are more limited, with oil-producing nations such as Saudi Arabia opposing a phase-out of fossil fuels.

"Geopolitics plays a huge role in the negotiations. The atmosphere can be a bit disheartening, but there are pockets of hope," says the Belgian negotiator Windey.

She specialises in the process of supporting populations as they face the financial challenges of the ecological transition.

It is a specific field, and one in which the negotiators all know one another, she says – allowing for progress that may not be reflected in the final, official declarations, Windey argues.

"We can speak frankly during informal talks," she says.

New EU guidelines urge citizens to manage the first 72 hours of an emergency independently. Commissioner Hadja Lahbib said it “has become an internationally recognised benchmark for household emergency preparedness.” Yet a University of Latvia survey found that only 8% feel prepared.

Food, water, and cash. Grab-and-go bags stocked with documents and medicines. Evacuation plans and practical skills, such as cooking without electricity and first aid.

This is how the European Commission’s new crisis guidelines advise citizens to be self-sufficient during the first 72 hours when cyber or drone attacks sabotage critical infrastructure and natural disasters disrupt transport and communication networks.

But few people are ready for a crisis breaking out today. The University of Latvia’s 2026 Baltic Individual Crisis Preparedness Barometer, which surveyed residents in 10 European cities across 8 Northern and Eastern EU countries (plus Iceland and Norway), found that just 8% feel quite or completely prepared. 44% plan to improve their preparedness within six months. 

Preparedness today

Self-sufficiency during the first 72 hours of a crisis is crucial, as “it reduces the pressure on emergency services and allows them to focus on those most in need,” Hadja Lahbib, EU Commissioner for Equality, Preparedness and Crisis Management, told Euronews.

Yet the Baltic Individual Crisis Preparedness Barometer shows that at least half of residents in every surveyed city feel unprepared today. Dr. Ieva Birka, the Barometer's lead researcher, is not surprised. What surprises her is that nothing is changing.  

“Preparedness has never been talked about more: there are national brochures, EU guidance and constant media coverage. Yet households’ actual material preparedness is not moving”, Birka explained.

Across the cities surveyed, only 31% have enough drinking water at home and 25% at work to last 72 hours or more. 50% think they have enough cash, and 71% believe they have enough food. While 73% have first-aid supplies, only 38% have a battery-powered AM/FM radio.

Differences between cities largely reflect how close people feel an attack is, Birka said. Vilnius is the only capital where the unprepared are a minority, as 67% consider an attack a major threat. But “feeling closer to the threat doesn’t mean being stocked up. Even in Vilnius, only about a quarter of respondents had three days’ worth of water,” she added.

Many people can’t afford

“Being prepared does not have to be expensive”, said Lahbib, suggesting that simple steps, including strong social networks and essentials such as food, water and a torch, can be real game-changers.

But many people can’t afford to be prepared. A family of four needs 36 litres of water for three days, non-perishable food, a battery-powered radio, first-aid supplies, medicines and cash. These essentials cost about €100–150 in Baltic capitals, while a fully stocked crisis kit with sleeping bags and tents can exceed €300, Birka explained. If heating fails, “unless you have a fireplace, the alternatives are generators or portable power stations, which cost hundreds of euros more”, she added.

About 30% of respondents say they need financial help to prepare. “Support should be targeted rather than universal,” Birka said, suggesting vouchers or ready-made kits for low-income households, distributed through municipalities and social services.

Asked whether the EU could fund preparedness, Lahbib said the Commission has launched “a behavioural study to better understand preparedness levels among low-income groups”. The results are expected next year.

When your preparedness depends on others

Money is not the only constraint. A 2026 European Disability Forum report, citing UN data, finds that 91% of people with disabilities in Europe lack a personal disaster plan, and 43% can’t evacuate without help. Accessible early warning systems cut the number to 22%, yet just 10% receive risk information in accessible formats like braille or sign language.

While the survey doesn’t include data specifically on people with disabilities or those who rely on assistive devices, Birka thinks “it's important to remember that for these groups, self-sufficiency depends on other people, so carers need to be prepared themselves.”

The Commission urges inclusive, accessible evacuations, transport, and shelters that meet diverse needs, with people with disabilities involved in planning. First-aid responders should be trained to communicate effectively, identify needs, and provide targeted support.

Birka wants these measures included in national and municipal emergency plans, not as "an optional extra”. She advises on personal emergency plans and support networks, voluntary registers of people who need assistance, backup power for medical and assistive devices, and accessible evacuation.

Preparedness is also psychological

For others, the issue is psychological. In Vilnius, where people feel the threat most heavily, 42% say the main obstacle is the psychological difficulty of thinking about it.

“More leaflets won’t close the gap,” Birka said, stressing that simply giving citizens more information about preparedness won't solve the problem. “People want more direct reassurance from governments that there is a plan, that crises will be handled, and that if individuals do their share in preparing, the country, civil protection and emergency services, and the army will do theirs”, she explained. 

Practical help is what makes the difference. For Birka, this includes concrete action plans and raising awareness in their own neighbourhoods. Formats should suit the audience, from short videos for younger generations to printed materials for older audiences.

Same guidelines, different levels of preparedness

The guidelines are non-binding. “Member States have been involved throughout,” Lahbib said, but “the EU cannot guarantee that citizens are ‘equally prepared’. That is the responsibility of each Member State.”

This could leave Europeans unevenly prepared and widen the existing gap between member states. Birka argued that consistently tracking progress across countries and over time can show whether national governments are taking the EU’s advice seriously.

The lead researcher urged the EU to adopt shared indicators and conduct regular, comparable surveys with clear, measurable targets, for example, tracking how many households have enough water for three days. “Shared standards for measuring and reporting would make progress visible and create healthy pressure to act”, said Birka.

Experts called for stricter regulation of digital platforms, warning that features designed to keep users online can fuel harmful internet use.

“Problematic” internet use has emerged as a major global public health concern, potentially affecting more than 10% of the world’s population and taking a substantial societal toll, experts warned.

Problematic usage of the internet (PUI) covers a wide range of behaviours, including gambling, gaming, pornography consumption, social media use and online shopping. These activities are not inherently harmful, but they are considered “problematic” when they interfere with daily life or rise to the level of a medical disorder, for example, gambling addiction.

In a report published in The Lancet Psychiatry, experts in public health, psychology and policy argued that governments should recognise PUI as a global public health concern and regulate the design features that keep people online, such as infinite scroll and autoplay.

“From a public health perspective, although many PUI- related behaviours might not reach the thresholds for clinical diagnosis, taken together, they constitute a substantial public health problem,” the authors wrote.

People with problematic internet use often also have mental health conditions such as attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), depression, anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), sleep disturbances, eating disorders, self-harm and suicidal ideation or attempts, the report said.

The report also linked PUI with interpersonal conflict, loneliness, family dysfunction, lower academic and work productivity and burnout.

Young people, those in low- and middle-income countries and people with mental health disorders appeared to be most at risk. It’s not clear whether PUI is becoming more common or if the consequences are simply becoming better understood.

Platform design increases the risk

While gambling, gaming and pornography existed long before the internet, the authors warned that digital platforms make these indulgences constantly accessible and have features that can make them addictive, such as algorithmic precision and real-time feedback.

Loneliness, poor family relations and spending more time online could all contribute to harmful behaviours.

However, the report said PUI could not be explained solely by individual vulnerabilities and was also shaped or amplified by the specific design features of online platforms and services, for example, social media algorithms.

Research on the issue is still underway, but the authors said there is enough evidence to justify a “precautionary approach” in public policy. They called for an internationally coordinated approach to address harms from PUI.

Current policy approaches may be insufficient. Social media bans that focus on age limits, for example, do not necessarily address the features that encourage compulsive internet use, such as infinite scrolls and push notifications, the report noted.

The authors argued that responsibility should lie with online platforms, not with individual users, and recommended holding those products to the same safety standards as tobacco, alcohol and gambling.

The report called for a range of actions, including restricting high-risk features, independent auditing of algorithms and binding rules on age limits and marketing restrictions.

The researchers urged governments to move away from voluntary industry self-regulation and towards enforceable standards that would make safety features the default and curb features designed to maximize engagement.

“The goal should be to prioritise public health over industry interests to reduce the societal harms of PUI,” the authors concluded.

An international team of scientists, including researchers from the University of Barcelona, has discovered a rare insect beside the remains of a glacier in Chilean Patagonia.

At the southern tip of Chilean Patagonia, near Cape Horn, the last remnants of a glacier have become the scene of an unexpected discovery. A group of scientists has found a rare insect on Navarino Island, a region where the ice is retreating and revealing a landscape in constant transformation.

The discovery is described in a study published in November 2026 in the scientific journal 'Ecology', which analyses ice loss in this area and records the presence of the insect. It is a stonefly, a type of insect closely linked to freshwater ecosystems. It belongs to the family Gripopterygidae, found in different regions of the southern hemisphere.

The researchers have not been able to match it to any known species, which raises the possibility that it could be a species not yet described by science. However, further studies will be needed to confirm this.

A discovery amid the thaw

The find was made next to the remnants of a glacier on Navarino Island, in the Tierra del Fuego archipelago, an area where the loss of ice is changing environmental conditions. Glaciers are not only part of the landscape. Meltwater from them feeds nearby ecosystems and creates particular conditions for numerous organisms. When the ice disappears, these environments also change.

For now, it is unknown whether the insect lives exclusively in this area or is also present in other parts of Patagonia. The study, titled "Rapid ice loss and a rare stonefly from Chile's southernmost glacier remnants" ("Rápida pérdida de hielo y un extraño plecóptero en los últimos vestigios glaciares del extremo sur de Chile", in Spanish), has not determined its conservation status either.

The research, led by Javier Rendoll-Cárcamo, involves scientists affiliated with institutions such as the University of Magallanes, the University of Barcelona and the British Antarctic Survey.

The Harvard study has revealed that pledges alone might not be enough, even as COP31 negotiators push for cleaner energy use in data centres.

For years, activists and experts have warned about the environmental impact of data centres. Now, a Harvard study has put an eye-opening figure on their carbon footprint.

According to researchers at the Ivy League university, the electricity consumed by 403 of the largest data centres in the US over one year generated about as much CO2 as Denmark – a country with a population of just six million.

In one of the first studies to estimate the electricity consumption and emissions of hyperscale data centres since the rise of AI, the researchers estimated their electricity consumption produced 25.7 million tonnes of CO2 between May 2024 and April 2025.

This is about two to three times higher than an earlier estimate based on 2018 data. More than half the power came from planet-warming fossil fuels, too – mostly natural gas and coal.

“We are going backwards toward the goal of controlling CO2 emissions,” Francesca Dominici, a Harvard biostatistics professor, told news agency AP.

The study comes just as COP31 negotiators launch a voluntary pledge, calling on data centre operators to use cleaner energy and disclose their environmental impact.

All the while, Europe is building up for its own data centre boom, too.

Europe’s data centre boom is underway

Within the next seven years, the EU wants to triple its data centre capacity as it seeks to compete in the global AI race. The building boom is already beginning. Property consultancy CBRE expects European capacity to grow by 20 per cent in 2026 alone.

While cities like London, Frankfurt and Paris have already become major hubs, electricity shortages have forced others – including Amsterdam and Dublin – to pause some new developments, prompting investors to look elsewhere to fill the void.

In Finland, 145 data centre projects have been announced nationwide in recent years – 60 this year alone. More than 50 are in the pipeline in Spain as well, 17 of which are already under construction.

Italy is attracting developers, too. In Puglia, local authorities have received 29 requests for electricity grid connections for potential data centres, while CBRE reports that Milan is expected to overtake Dublin as Europe’s fifth-largest data centre market by 2028.

Data centre construction comes at a cost

The IEA estimates data centres will account for 10 per cent of additional electricity demand in the EU by 2030, putting a strain on its aging power grids.

Residents have also raised major concerns about water consumption, noise pollution and the amount of land being given over to data centres – among other fears.

In July, the UK government overruled a local council to approve a €585 million plan to convert the former Truman Brewery in east London into a mixed-use development, including shops, offices, homes and a data centre.

Campaigners took to the streets in protest, saying the data centre alone could consume as much electricity as 15,000 homes. But the project would create just 44 new homes – and only six for social housing.

In October, more than 1,000 people representing about 40 local committees gathered in Milan to protest Italy’s data centre expansion and demand a halt to new developments.

Less than a month later, activists broke into a Microsoft construction site in Amsterdam, climbing a crane, setting off flares and clashing with police.

Then, in November, Stop Dirty Data Centres – a coalition of more than 100 environmental, digital rights and community groups – organised demonstrations in 15 countries to demand a freeze on new data centres until governments address their impact on utility bills, housing and resources.

How Europe plans to reduce the environmental impact

The Harvard researchers found that a data centre’s footprint largely depends on where it is built. For example, the same amount of electricity generated more than twice as much carbon in the state of Wyoming, where the power mostly comes from coal, than in Oregon, where hydropower is a sizable part of the energy mix.

They also found that operators rarely disclose their electricity consumption, making it difficult to calculate their emissions individually.

The EU hopes to avoid similar stumbling blocks.

Under the Energy Efficiency Directive, data centres using at least 500 kilowatts of computing power must report their energy and water consumption.

In September, the European Commission proposed A-to-G ratings for energy and water efficiency, similar to what is used to label household appliances.

Some operators claim to be finding ways to reduce their impact, too.

In Portugal, for example, Start Campus is developing a 1.2-gigawatt data centre complex in Sinesthat uses seawater for cooling. And in Helsinki, the city’s municipal energy company plans to recover enough excess heat from a new data centre to keep about 70,000 apartments warm annually once it is fully operational.

Euronews breaks down the European Commission's new proposal to issue a €45 billion support loan to Ukraine. Here's what you need to know.

The European Union is "as committed as ever to support Ukraine in war and in peace", Ursula von der Leyen said as she unveiled a €45 billion support loan to help the country address its growing wartime budget deficit.

"We think this is the best way to give Ukraine a strong hand at the negotiation table," the European Commission president said on Wednesday.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly thanked her, saying "strong support for Ukraine is the best signal to Russia that this war must end".

The loan still has to be greenlit by EU leaders, but the urgency is growing. Moscow's non-stop airstrikes have multiplied costs and worsened Kyiv's dependency on foreign aid.

But governments are also wary of the optics of approving fresh cash for Ukraine at a time of high energy bills, tight budgets and popular discontent. After all, any new pledges will fall on European taxpayers.

Here is everything you need to know about the new loan.

Why now?

In December last year, EU leaders agreed on a €90 billion loan to fulfil Ukraine's military and financial needs for 2026 and 2027 combined.

The €90 billion loan, which is still ongoing, was designed under the assumption that Russia's war would end sometime in 2026.

Instead, the opposite has happened: Moscow has escalated its attacks to make Ukraine's winter insufferable and further cripple the country's economy.

The relentless attacks have disrupted business activity, impaired the energy system and diminished Kyiv's capacity to raise public revenue. The blockade in the Black Sea, a vital route for Ukrainian farmers, has further exacerbated the pain.

The devastation has drilled a €70 billion hole in Ukraine's 2027 budget. In their October summit, leaders heard from Zelenskyy and agreed to address the situation.

Why €45 billion?

This is the division of labour between the EU and its allies.

Last year, the bloc committed to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's estimated €135 billion needs. This produced the €90 billion loan.

Now, it repeats the same formula: the €45 billion will cover two-thirds of the €70 billion shortfall. Other allies, such as the UK, Norway, Canada, Japan and Australia, are expected to supply the remaining €25 billion.

In its proposal, the Commission offers two ways for allies to chip in: a €5 billion top-up through AAA-rated guarantees or an extension of a previous G7 loan backed by the windfall profits stemming from the immobilised Russian assets.

There is little hope that the US will contribute financially, despite the Democratic Party's sweeping victory in the midterm elections.

"It would not be wise to budget on hope alone," a senior Commission official quipped.

How will it be raised?

The €45 billion will be raised through joint debt, a straightforward option.

The Commission, which is triple-rated, will issue bonds of different maturities to the markets and gradually borrow the money on behalf of all member states.

This is the same method as in the €90 billion loan.

Combined, the EU will raise €135 billion for Ukraine in 2026 and 2027.

How much will it cost?

Joint debt is always costly – even more so today.

Borrowing costs have soared worldwide in reaction to energy turmoil, geopolitical volatility, high debt concerns and the all-consuming AI race. From Brussels to Washington, public accounting is under strain.

Commission officials estimate an annual bill of roughly €6 billion in interest payments: €3.5 billion from the €90 billion loan (up from €3 billion when it was set up) and somewhere between €2 billion and €2.5 billion from the €45 billion loan.

Member states will subsidise the interest to avoid burdening Ukraine.

As of now, the plan is to pay the annual payments through the €100 billion special envelope that Brussels has allocated for Ukraine in the next seven-year budget. But this will reduce the allocation by €42 billion and slash fungible support for Kyiv.

An alternative plan would be to cover the payments through a separate financial instrument to keep the €100 billion envelope intact.

The question adds yet another link between Ukraine and the budget, which are rapidly becoming one single, politically explosive package. Both depend on unanimity

What about those countries that want an opt-out?

In the lead-up to the presentation, four member states – Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria – indicated they will not be part of the new scheme.

"I say a clear no to war, weapons and war loans, and a yes to peace," Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said in a video message.

Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary are already exempted from the €90 billion and want to continue their opt-out policy. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev, a vocal critic of weapon deliveries to Ukraine, wants to join the club.

The attitude has infuriated German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who argues that "supporting Ukraine is a matter of our indivisible European security, and so must be the burden sharing for that support".

Merz has threatened to veto the next EU budget, which contains billions in cohesion funds that Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria depend on, if the new loan is not backed by all 27 member states.

"I support the Chancellor," von der Leyen said, taking Merz's side. "I'm very confident we will agree by 27."

The Commission has offered the four countries the option to opt in to the loan's budget strand (€20 billion) and opt out of its military strand (€25 billion). But this is unlikely to sway them, as their opposition is intrinsically political.

Will it ever be repaid?

The EU will ask Ukraine to repay either the €90 billion or the €45 billion loans only when Russia agrees to provide war reparations as part of a future peace deal.

Until that day comes, it will roll over the loans indefinitely.

Moscow has repeatedly dismissed such a thing, raising the odds that the EU will have to assume responsibility one way or another.

Brussels says it "reserves the right" to use the immobilised Russian assets, worth €210 billion, to repay the aid provided to Ukraine. But this will deprive Kyiv of a much-needed cash injection to rebuild the country after the war ends.

Ukraine, which is already saddled with debts from other partners and institutions, is not expected to pay out of pocket in any case.

"There can always be a political decision to waive the debt," a senior official said.

"De facto, the EU has become the lender of last resort for Ukraine and is likely to be there for some time."

Get the festive season on the right track with these unique European winter and Christmas rail journeys, offering luxury, adventure and slow travel.

With picture-perfect snowy scenes, twinkling lights, hearty feasts and so many Christmas markets to enjoy, winter is a great time of year to visit Europe.

And what better way to get in the holiday spirit than with a slow rail journey through some of the continent’s most beautiful landscapes?

Here, Euronews Travel rounds up some of the most picturesque and unique festive train journeys to take this winter.

The Santa Claus Express, Finland

This might be one of Europe’s most magical train journeys to take at the end of the year. Venture straight into the heart of Christmas fairy tales with the Santa Claus Express, a Finnish double-decker night train which takes travellers from Helsinki and Turku all the way north into the Arctic Circle. Going past frozen lakes and snow-dusted woods, some lucky travellers may also spot the elusive Northern Lights during certain journeys.

By the time you wake up, you’ll be deep into Finnish Lapland in Rovaniemi, the “official hometown of Santa Claus”. Here, travellers can enjoy attractions such as Santa Claus Village, and go to the Santa Claus Main Post Office to get an Arctic Circle postmark available on letters and postcards. You can also post letters from here.

The train offers standard sleeper cabins, deluxe sleeper cabins and seating carriages. Sleeper cabins usually have two beds, temperature control and private bathroom options with showers. A dining car with breakfast, other meals and snack options is also available.

Cogwheel train to Santa’s House, Switzerland

From the shores of Lake Geneva, a cogwheel train climbs from Montreux to Santa’s House at Rochers-de-Naye, more than 2,000 metres above sea level. The 55-minute ride offers views over the lake and the Swiss Alps, and children can meet Santa and have their photo taken with him at the summit. The festive trips run on selected dates from 20 November to 24 December 2026. A combined ticket covers the return train journey, a reserved seat on the way up and entry to Santa’s House.

La Dolce Vita Orient Express ‘Jingle Route’

Luxury sleeper train La Dolce Vita Orient Express is running a festive round trip from Rome via Venice and Florence. Departing on 19 December 2026, the three-day, two-night “Jingle Route” begins at Ostiense Station in Rome before travelling north through Italy's winter landscapes and arriving in Venice in the early evening.

Here, private boats escort guests through the canals to the recently opened Orient Express Venezia hotel where they can enjoy a festive celebration with live music and dinner in the palazzo before returning to the train just after midnight.

On day two, passengers arrive in Florence in the afternoon and have time to explore the city before returning to the train for dinner and live entertainment. A slow journey will then see the train make its way back to Ostiense Station where the journey ends the following morning. Prices start from €6,560 per passenger.

Majestic Imperator ‘Advent in Prague’

The Majestic Imperator is running a festive round trip from Vienna to Prague from 4-6 December 2026. The luxury train leaves Vienna on the Friday morning, with a champagne brunch and live music on board before arriving in the Czech capital that afternoon. Passengers spend two nights at the five-star Almanac Prague hotel near Wenceslas Square.

On the Saturday, monks lead a private tour of the library at Strahov Monastery, followed by a concert. The train heads back to Vienna on the Sunday evening, with a three-course dinner and live music. The package costs €1,250 per person, including the hotel stay.

British Pullman, UK

On 28 November and 10 December, Belmond’s British Pullman train heads from London to Bath for a day at the city’s Christmas market. Passengers are served brunch on the way out and a four-course dinner with wine on the return, with time in between to browse the market’s craft stalls.

The luxury train’s festive programme also includes a trip to Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire for its illuminated light trail and a day in Canterbury that pairs a Christmas carol performance with time to explore the city. For a trip centred on the food, the Christmas lunch round trip serves a festive meal as the train rolls through the countryside.

Bergen Railway, Norway

The Bergen Railway, operated by the Norwegian state-owned rail company Vy, is another train line that comes into its own in winter. From Oslo to the city of Bergen on Norway’s west coast, this train travels around 500 kilometres in about seven hours and includes about 180 tunnels. It is also one of Europe’s most high-altitude lines.

Enjoy a magical festive winter adventure, as you pass by frozen vistas and waterfalls, snowfields, dramatic mountains, winding fjords, vast plateaus and fairy tale-like villages with wooden houses.

Some highlights of the route include the Hardangervidda plateau, one of Europe’s largest mountain plateaus, as well as Finse, a high-altitude station with stunning glacier views and Geilo, a popular ski resort town. Travellers can connect to the famous Flåm Railway at Myrdal station for an even more unforgettable descent into the fjords.

Passengers can choose between multiple daily departures, including a sleeper train. The train offers a first and second class, as well as a cafe car, vending machines, and wi-fi. Some carriages are also specially designed for families.

Golden Eagle Danube Express ‘Christmas Markets of Central Europe’

Love Christmas markets? The Golden Eagle Danube Express is for you. Offering a variety of year-round itineraries ranging from eight to 12 days, this train is extra special in winter. It runs a “Christmas Markets of Central Europe” itinerary, which operates between Budapest and Munich, taking in Vienna, the Austrian Alps and Salzburg as well.

Departing on 3 December 2026, this eight-day trip includes a two-night stay at a five-star hotel in Budapest, three nights on the train and two hotel nights in Munich, as well as welcome dinners, guided city tours, champagne receptions, and Christmas market tours.

Highlights include a traditional horse-drawn carriage ride in Vienna, a concert of Viennese Christmas folk songs and a tasting of Pirker gingerbread.

Glacier Express

The Glacier Express route is one of Switzerland’s most famous rail journeys. Dubbed the “slowest express train in the world”, it runs between Zermatt and St. Moritz in an epic eight-hour journey over 291 kilometres. Cross the Swiss Alps, passing through 91 tunnels and 291 bridges, while marvelling at panoramic snow-capped mountain views, icy blue lakes and deep gorges.

Highlights include the dramatic Rhine Gorge, also known as the “Swiss Grand Canyon”, and the Landwasser Viaduct, a UNESCO World Heritage-listed railway. Choose from three classes, including second class, first class and excellence class.

The train includes facilities such as wi-fi access, digital infotainment and audio guides. Excellence class passengers can enjoy luxurious five-course dining, with vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free and lactose-free options as well as a range of regional Swiss wines and digestifs. All meals are freshly prepared on board, with high-quality, seasonal ingredients and are served at your seat. Winter service resumes on 5 December 2026 and seat reservations are mandatory.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday that he expects US envoys to brief him on the talks taking place in China, as Donald Trump prepares to meet China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin.

Trump has said he plans to raise limits on nuclear weapons and an end to the war in Ukraine in his historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

Germany, France and Britain are co-hosting talks in Berlin that begin only hours after Trump, Putin and Xi wrap up their landmark trilateral summit in Shenzhen.

Anthropic priced its record IPO at $83 a share ahead of Thursday's debut, as Nvidia heads for a seventh weekly loss and Washington tightens AI chip exports.

For years, Jensen Huang and Dario Amodei could hardly agree on anything.

The Nvidia founder once said he disagreed "with almost everything" the Anthropic chief executive says. Amodei, for his part, compared selling advanced American chips to China to "selling nuclear weapons to North Korea".

This week, their paths split dramatically. Huang is gone from the company he built over 33 years, while Amodei is taking his to Wall Street in what could become the largest stock market debut in history.

Anthropic, the San Francisco company behind the Claude chatbot, priced its shares at $83 each on Wednesday and increased the size of the offering, according to people familiar with the matter. That is well above the $70 to $78 range set in its filings with US regulators.

At that price, the 825 million shares originally on offer alone would raise more than $68bn. A private placement at the same price with investors including Nvidia, Google and AMD adds at least $26bn more, taking the total past the $86.2bn SpaceX raised in June, including extra shares sold to meet demand.

Shares are expected to start trading on Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. Counting all its shares, the company would be worth about $1.5tn.

A company that grew 45 times in 18 months

In the first quarter of 2025, the company booked $376 million in revenue. In the third quarter of 2026, it booked $16.96bn, an increase of 1,127% compared with the same period a year earlier.

The pace has not slowed. Anthropic's annualised revenue, a company estimate based on recent usage and subscriptions, reached $81bn at the end of October, $10bn more than just a month earlier.

Most of that money comes from businesses, and more than 11,900 customers now spend over $100,000 a year.

The cost of serving them is also falling. A year ago, computing power cost Anthropic one and a half times its revenue. In the third quarter of 2026, it was 58% of revenue.

Its $104bn net loss for the first nine months of the year comes almost entirely from accounting revaluations that disappear with the listing. Excluding stock-based pay and donations, operations made a $2.5bn profit in the third quarter.

Wall Street sees a catalyst, with a price tag

Analysts see the debut as a test for the whole artificial intelligence trade.

"The issue is over six times subscribed, and there's plenty of excitement ahead of the first public offering of a pure frontier lab at the forefront of AI development," David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation, said in a note on Wednesday.

Thahbib Rahman, research analyst at Block Scholes, sees a familiar pattern. Bitcoin fell 19% in the 50 days before SpaceX began trading in June, and it is down 23% over the same stretch ahead of Anthropic.

Yet Rahman said "there is some evidence to suggest that this latest sell-off is more closely tied to the wider rout in risk assets than to investors rotating out of crypto assets and into the IPO".

Jay Peters, portfolio manager at NewEdge Wealth, considers the price fair. "It's a historic IPO and we think the valuation at $1.2-1.4T is reasonable based on the trajectory of the business," he said in emailed comments.

"Anthropic is coming on Thursday - all aboard!" said Richard Reyle, chief investment officer at Questar Capital Partners, who called Nvidia "the Jenga tower of the whole AI trade".

Nvidia's worst losing streak since 2008

Nvidia shares fell 2.9% on Wednesday to $150.96, the day after its quarterly results. The stock is heading for a seventh straight weekly loss, its longest losing streak since July 2008, and has lost about 35% of its value since the start of October.

The slide deepened after Nvidia announced Huang's resignation on 12 November, following reports about his private life that had prompted an internal investigation. Chief financial officer Colette Kress is now interim CEO.

Its results on Tuesday beat expectations, but did little to calm investors.

"Investors have, repeatedly and ultimately, 'bought the dip' on every occasion since October 2022. So far, this one hasn't worked out so well," Morrison said.

Washington tightens the chip pipeline

Politics is adding to the pressure. On Monday, the US Commerce Department introduced licence requirements for advanced chips shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, which it considers at higher risk of diversion.

It also requires licences for data centres anywhere that rent large amounts of computing power to Chinese companies.

It is the kind of restriction Amodei has long called for, and one Huang has spent years fighting.

Peters sees the market moving towards "a slower-for-longer buildout", as borrowing costs rise and politics gets tougher.

The buyer becomes the investor

For three years, the AI boom rewarded the companies selling the hardware.

On Thursday, the market will put a price for the first time on a frontier AI lab, one of the handful of companies building the most advanced models.

And one of the buyers lining up next to ordinary investors is Nvidia itself, ready to put more than $10bn into the company whose chief executive its founder spent years arguing with.

Whether Thursday becomes a turning point or a high-water mark will depend less on the first day of trading than on what Anthropic reports in the quarters that follow.

• Parlamentul României a eliminat treptat singura etapă a controlului democratic în care directorul Serviciului Român de Informații (SRI) era obligat să dea socoteală public pentru activitatea instituției.  
  • De 21 de ani, niciun director SRI nu a mai răspuns în plenul Parlamentului la întrebările senatorilor și deputaților. Până în 2005, însă, șeful serviciului era chestionat ore întregi de la tribună despre subiecte sensibile: foști securiști, interceptări ilegale, corupție sau presiuni asupra justiției.
  • Stenogramele ședințelor de plen din 1997 până în 2023, analizate de PressOne, arată că dezbaterea rapoartelor de activitate ale SRI a scăzut de la circa cinci ore la doar opt minute. 
  • Din 2013, de când directorul SRI nu a mai călcat în plenul Parlamentului – dezvăluire făcută în primul episod al acestei investigații –, au dispărut și explicațiile publice în legătură cu activitatea serviciului și cu felul în care acesta își folosește puterile excepționale încredințate de stat. 
  • Astfel, niciuna dintre marile controverse în care a fost implicat serviciul în ultimii peste zece ani nu a mai fost dezbătută în plen: de la fuga lui Sebastian Ghiță de sub filajul polițiștilor, la negocierile politice pentru formarea guvernului purtate în prezența directorului SRI, Eduard Hellvig, sau anularea alegerilor din 2024.
  • În episodul de astăzi, PressOne reconstituie cum se făcea controlul parlamentar pe vremea când directorii SRI veneau în plen să prezinte rapoartele de activitate și pune în lumină ce se pierde astăzi, când cel mai mare serviciu de informații al țării a ieșit de sub controlul legislativului. 

Timp de un deceniu după căderea comunismului, dezbaterea raportului anual al SRI era momentul în care directorul serviciului urca la tribuna Parlamentului și răspundea public la întrebările senatorilor și deputaților.

Stenogramele ședințelor de plen din 1997 până în 2023, analizate de PressOne, arată cum acest exercițiu de control democratic s-a degradat de la o legislatură la alta, iar Parlamentul și-a cedat treptat prerogativele publice de verificare a celui mai mare serviciu de informații din România.

Deși legea privind organizarea și funcționarea SRI îl obligă pe director să prezinte Parlamentului rapoartele anuale de activitate, acesta s-a sustras controlului democratic cu complicitatea șefilor celor două camere legislative, iar din 2013 niciun șef al serviciului nu a mai dat socoteală în fața senatorilor și deputaților.

Nouă rapoarte de activitate ale SRI au fost doar trecute pe ordinea de zi, fără să mai fie prezentate aleșilor și fără să fie dezbătute de către aceștia, așa cum a dezvăluit PressOne în primul episod al acestei investigații. 

Contrastul între practica de control prezentă și cea din anii ‘90 este frapant. 

În 1997, raportul prezentat în plen chiar de directorul SRI a fost singurul subiect al ședinței. Dezbaterea a durat peste cinci ore, iar 16 parlamentari i-au adresat acestuia zeci de întrebări. 

Ședința din anul 2000 a durat și ea peste patru ore, iar discuțiile pe marginea activității SRI erau încă un punct major pe ordinea de zi.

Pentru comparație, în 2023 – când pe ordinea de zi a plenului a fost inclus pentru ultima oară un raport de activitate al SRI – timpul s-a redus la doar opt minute. 

De-a lungul anilor, rapoartele de activitate ale SRI au început să ajungă în plen tot mai rar și tot mai târziu, iar odată cu întârzierea lor s-a schimbat și modul în care au fost aduse la cunoștință senatorilor și deputaților. 

De la două rapoarte prezentate simultan, numărul acestora a crescut la trei, apoi la câte cinci sau chiar șase într-o singură ședință, astfel că parlamentarii au ajuns să discute despre activitatea SRI la patru, cinci sau chiar șase ani după perioada acoperită de rapoarte.
